body.heading: It starts with the molecule
paragraphs: Water molecules link together at particular angles, and when water freezes, those links settle into rings of six. Ice, at the molecular level, is a hexagonal crystal — and the snowflake simply grows that pattern up to a size you can see.
So the six sides are not a decoration added later. They are the molecule’s geometry, magnified millions of times.

body.heading: Growing in the cloud
paragraphs: A snowflake begins as a tiny crystal around a speck of dust high in a winter cloud. As it drifts and falls, water vapour freezes onto it, and the six corners — sticking out slightly farther into the moist air — grow fastest, sprouting arms.

The exact shape depends on temperature and humidity, which change as the flake falls. Plates, needles, columns and the classic branching stars are all the same crystal following different weather. Each flake’s pattern is, in effect, a diary of its journey down.

body.heading: No two alike?
paragraphs: In the 1880s, Wilson Bentley, a Vermont farmer, became the first person to photograph a snowflake, and went on to capture thousands — no two exactly alike. Simple, tiny crystals can match, but a large, branching flake has so many details that a repeat is effectively impossible.
Six sides, guaranteed. The rest is weather, chance and a long fall through cold air.

takeaway: Six sides come from how water molecules lock together in ice — the endless variety comes from each flake’s unique trip through the cloud.
